theme: Covenant concluded; the Sabbath; ratification with blood
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 23:1-24:18. The first part finishes the Book of the Covenant with laws on justice, the Sabbath, and the feasts. The second part, chapter 24, describes the ratification of the covenant with blood. Read chapter 24 slowly. It is one of the most important chapters in the Old Testament.
settingTheScene: The laws of the Book of the Covenant are almost finished. Now Moses goes down to the people, and the covenant between God and Israel is formally sealed. This is like a wedding ceremony or a treaty ratification. There is a reading of the terms, a public promise by the people, a sacrifice, and a meal. Then Moses is called back up the mountain for forty days to receive instructions for the tabernacle. This is the end of the first half of Exodus, and the unit’s closing scene.
observation: “You shall not fall in with the many to do wrong, nor shall you bear witness in a lawsuit, siding with the many, so as to pervert justice” (23:2).
“If you meet your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray, you shall bring it back to him” (23:4).
“You shall not oppress a sojourner. You know the heart of a sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt” (23:9).
“Six days you shall do your work, but on the seventh day you shall rest” (23:12). The land too is to rest every seventh year (23:10-11).
Three times a year, all males are to appear before the LORD at the feasts of unleavened bread, harvest, and ingathering (23:14-17).
God promises to send an angel before them, “for my name is in him” (23:20-21).
Moses writes down all the words of the LORD and builds an altar with twelve pillars. The people say, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient” (24:3-7).

Moses takes half the blood and throws it against the altar, and the other half he sprinkles on the people, saying, “Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words” (24:6-8).
Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders go up and “saw the God of Israel…they beheld God, and ate and drank” (24:9-11).
Moses goes up the mountain with Joshua, and the glory of the LORD rests on it like “a devouring fire” for forty days and forty nights (24:13-18).
interpretation:
The laws at the start of chapter 23 are some of the most practical in the Bible. They tell the truth in court, even when the crowd is against you. They tell you to help an enemy’s animal in trouble. They forbid taking bribes. The standards are high and they touch real life. The line “You shall not fall in with the many to do wrong” is a good motto for a believer in any age. The right thing and the popular thing are not always the same.

Most striking is the repeated appeal to Israel’s own experience. “You know the heart of a sojourner.” The law is built on empathy: you have been where they are, so treat them as God treated you. This is the way the Bible teaches ethics. It asks people to remember grace and then to act like people who have received it.

Now to chapter 24, which is the most significant. The covenant is sealed with blood. This is the second great blood ritual in the book, after the Passover. At the Passover, the blood protected Israel from judgment. Here, the blood binds Israel to God in covenant. Half is thrown on the altar, which represents God, and half is sprinkled on the people. Both parties are bound together by the blood. “Behold the blood of the covenant.” These are words that Jesus will echo at the Last Supper.

The promise of the people, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient,” is sincere. But as you saw earlier, they will break it within weeks. The covenant is real, and the people are weak. This tension, between God’s holy demands and human inability, runs through the whole Old Testament and creates the longing for a better covenant.

The scene on the mountain in verses 9 to 11 is one of the most mysterious in the Bible. Leaders of Israel see the God of Israel. They see “under his feet as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness.” It is a glimpse of the throne room of God. And, astonishingly, “God did not lay his hand on them. They beheld God, and ate and drank.” They share a meal in his presence. This is a preview of the fellowship that is the goal of the covenant, and it will be fulfilled when God’s people eat and drink with him in the kingdom.

The unit ends with Moses entering the cloud. The glory looks like a devouring fire. God is both near and dangerous, and Moses will be gone for forty days.
connection: At the Last Supper, Jesus took the cup and said, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28), echoing Exodus 24:8. Hebrews 9:18-22 explains that the first covenant was inaugurated with blood and that Christ’s blood inaugurates a better one. The meal on the mountain points to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Peter says that believers are “sprinkled with his blood” (1 Peter 1:2).
application:
When you take the Lord’s Supper, hear the words of Exodus 24:8 behind the words of Jesus. You are being brought into a covenant sealed with blood.

Think about where you tend to “fall in with the many.” Ask God for courage to stand for what is right.

Remember what it was like to be a stranger or an outsider in a new church, a new job, or a new town. Reach out to someone who is new this week.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for the blood that sealed the covenant for you.
Ask for courage to do right when the crowd does wrong.
Ask him to teach you kindness to strangers.
